newsitem.title: UK: British Aerospace wins Australian Hawk order.
newsitem.headline: British Aerospace wins Australian Hawk order.

text.p: British Aerospace Plc said on Monday that the Australian government had picked it to supply Hawk fighter training aircraft to the Australian airforce.

The company put no value on the deal, but industry sources said total costs could rise to 1.0 billion pounds ($1.65 billion) over the lifetime of the project, which covers the supply of up to 40 aircraft.

In Canberra, Australian defence minister Ian McLachlan said BAe had been chosen as the "potential supplier" for new trainng jets, which BAe said meant theirs was the preferred tender for the contract.
BAe said that production of the aircraft would begin in early 1997 with handover of the first aircraft by mid-1999. The first 12 will be built in Britain and the rest assembled in Australia.
The aircraft is a special version of the Hawk 100 series, with a cockpit modified to minimise conversion training for pilots moving on to McDonnell Douglas F/A-18 fighters.
BAe beat Italy's Aermacchi, which had offered its MB.399FD trainer, in the competition to win the order. McDonnell Douglas, with a U.S. Navy version of the Hawk, was eliminated in September.

"All tenders were of a high quality and British Aerospace's bid was selected after detailed evaluation across a wide range of areas, including aircraft design and performance, costs and Australian industry involvement proposals," McLachlan said.
The Hawks will replace elderly Aermacchi MB.326s for introductory training of combat jet pilots and for exercising with the Royal Australian Navy.
Selection of the Hawk takes to 15 the number of countries that have ordered the aircraft or had it delivered to them, with orders or known requirements totalling around 750 aircraft.
BAe shares were up eight pence at 11.57 pounds in late morning trade. ($1=.6067 Pound)
